definition: The physical parts of a cigar and their roles: filler, binder, wrapper, cap, head, foot, and shoulder.
The burnt end of a lit cigar; its color (white, grey, black) reflects soil minerals such as magnesium.
The often colorful ring of paper around the head of a cigar identifying the brand and country of origin, often with intricate lithography.
The leaf that holds the filler leaves together inside a cigar; often a wrapper-grade leaf downgraded for cosmetic imperfections; with the filler it forms the bunch.
The small leaf that covers and secures the head of the cigar; it must be cut or removed before smoking.
related: cigars.Cigar Production.Flag Tip; cigars.Cigar Production.Gum; cigars.Cigar Production.Triple Cap; cigars.Storage and Smoking.Cold Draw; cigars.Storage and Smoking.Cutter

definition: The innermost leaves of a cigar, surrounded by the binder; premium handmades use between two and five filler leaves.
The end of the cigar that is lit.
The end of the cigar that goes in the mouth, enclosed by the cap.
The desirable oily sheen on a wrapper leaf, a sign of adequate humidification; more common on dark wrappers such as Maduro and Oscuro.
The part of a cigar where the body curves to meet the cap; cut above it so the cap stays intact.
Tiny bumps on a cigar's wrapper leaf formed by oil pockets; common on Cameroon wrappers.
The rib of a tobacco leaf that delivers nutrients; pronounced veins are undesirable on wrapper leaves.
The outermost and highest-quality leaf of a premium cigar; the most expensive leaf, ideally free of veins, tears, and cosmetic imperfections.
scope_note: Some references credit the wrapper with contributing up to 60% of a cigar's flavor, in addition to its dominant role in appearance and aroma.
related: cigars.Tobacco Cultivation.Shade Grown; cigars.Tobaccos and Origins.Connecticut Shade

definition: Terms from cigar culture and the trade: slang, aficionado practices, brands, and commerce.
A recipe of herbs, wine, rum, or liqueurs used to infuse tobaccos.
The clearance aisle or shelf, physical or online, for cigars marked down to the lowest possible prices; a buzz word for bargain hunters.
A term once used for small-batch releases from makers outside the mainstream; overuse has eroded it as a romantic classification.

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.Brother Of The Leaf
definition: A popular contemporary term identifying a fellow cigar lover; usage has blossomed across the Internet.
A small US cigar factory from before the Cuban Revolution; the term originates from Ohio-grown tobacco, the Buckeye State.
Slang for a small cigar factory or shop.

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.Cigar Association of America
definition: An organization of importers, distributors, and manufacturers of cigars.
A bar or lounge where cigar smoking is permitted.
The period of tremendous growth in the premium cigar industry from the early to late 1990s, when demand quadrupled from 100 million to over 400 million cigars.

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.Cigar Box Tool
definition: The simple tool used to break cigar box seals in retail shops, removing the nail that seals a flat-top box and pounding it back in.
A case designed to protect cigars during travel or transport, ranging from pocket sizes holding one to three cigars to larger models storing ten or more.
A room or area where cigar smoking is permitted, primarily found inside premium cigar retail shops.

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.Cigar Rights of America
definition: An organization established in 2008 by cigar companies, retailers, and consumers to promote and protect the rights of premium cigar lovers.
A cigar manufactured in the US prior to the Cuban Embargo, made with Cuban tobacco.
A discontinued brand or blend that will no longer be made, removed from the market quickly at dramatically lowered prices.
The government-owned enterprise that controls all of Cuba's cigar brands.

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.Federal Excise Tax
definition: The tax levied on cigars imported into the US; the 2009 SCHIP expansion raised it from under 5 cents to 40.26 cents per cigar.

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.Glass Top Cohibas
definition: A reference to commonly counterfeited Cuban Cohibas: real ones are never packaged in boxes with a clear window displaying the cigars.
A complimentary Cuban term for a farmer or man of the earth.
A traditional Cuban dress shirt lined with many front pockets, worn untucked.
The company in charge of global distribution for Cuban cigars.
The International Premium Cigar & Pipe Retailers Association, formerly the Retail Tobacco Dealers of America: a US trade organization of premium tobacco retailers.
synonyms: International Premium Cigar & Pipe Retailers Association; RTDA; Retail Tobacco Dealers of America

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.La Casa Del Habano
definition: Cigar shops that sell Cuban cigars and are partially owned by Habanos S.A.

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.Pre Castro Cigar
definition: A Cuban cigar manufactured prior to Fidel Castro's ascent to power in January 1959.

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.Pre Embargo Cigar
definition: A Cuban cigar manufactured before the enactment of the US trade embargo against Cuba in 1962.
Cuban cigars released only in specific regions.
The State Children's Health Care Initiative Program, whose 2009 expansion was funded by the federal excise tax on cigars.
The unit of measure for a single cigar, as opposed to a box.
A cigar made in very small quantities, often due to the rarity of its tobaccos; unlike a limited edition it may be produced annually.
Slang term for a cigar.

fqn: cigars.Cigar Culture and Commerce.Suggested Retail Price
definition: The price a manufacturer or distributor charges for a cigar; federal excise tax is often included, but state and local taxes are not, so prices vary by state.
The Cuban term for a tobacco grower.
Cigar Aficionado's annual Top 25 Cigars of the Year list, announced at the end of the year.
A tobacco plantation.
A sampler featuring numerous sizes of one single cigar blend — an opportunity to taste how different shapes present a blend.
Packaging formats and materials for cigars: boxes, tubes, cellophane, bundles, and cedar.
The layer of paper or film that folds protectively over the cigars inside a dress box, typically featuring the brand's logo.
The formally styled cedar cigar box: two hinges, a clasp, dovetailed joints, and four lifted cedar collars forming an inner lip.
The traditional cigar package, widely credited to H. Upmann in the early 1800s; US law since 1865 requires wooden boxes in counts of 25, 50, 100, or 250; Spanish cedar is the most common material.
A code, found predominantly on the bottom of Cuban boxes, used to identify the age of the cigars; uncommon outside Cuba.
The clasp that fastens the top of a cigar box lid to the bottom.
Cigars packaged wrapped in cellophane instead of boxes, commonly in counts of 20 or 25; once for un-banded seconds, now also an economy premium format.
A packaging style of 25 or 50 cigars in Spanish cedar boxes, bound with a ribbon inside; the extra air between cigars is believed to facilitate aging.
A long, thin strip of cedar that is lit and then used to light a cigar, transferring no impurities from fuel or matches.
The thin, clear protective sleeve around individual cigars; safeguards packaging, transport, and retail handling, and inhibits humidity loss.
An individual box for a single cigar.
The Spanish cedar slats that line the interior edges of a cigar box and form an inner lip.
The sides of a cigar box that bear the brand's name, logo, and other visual elements.
The outer lid or top of a cigar box.
A traditional packing of 25 cigars in a box: 8 on the bottom row, 9 in the middle, 8 on top.
A decorative and protective wrap, often covering a portion of a cigar, that can also encapsulate flavor as it ages.
A vintage packaging form: heavy glass jars of 25 or 50 cigars, rarely used today.
A bundle of 50 cigars, traditionally tied with a ribbon.
The front side of a cigar box where the brand name, logo, and decorative elements appear.
A rectangular or oval sticker on the top of a cigar box, wrapping around to the bottom, that must be sliced to open the lid.
A plain cedar cigar box with a clasp on the front and two rear hinges.
A cabinet-selection-style box with a sliding lid, typically containing 25 or 50 ribbon-bound cigars.
Cedrela, a mahogany-family tree harvested in tropical regions; ideal for cigar boxes and humidors because it reacts positively with moisture and benefits aging; also a tasting note.
The sticker that conceals the nail in the lid of a box of cigars.
A rectangular box format with 12 cigars plus a space holder on the bottom row and 13 on top, usually sealed with a brass nail.
The ornamental elements that embellish the edges of cigar boxes.
A glass or aluminum container for an individual cigar, protecting it in a pocket or suitcase; tubed cigars are often wrapped in cedar.
The inner portion of a cigar box lid, often adorned with the brand's logo or ornate artwork.
A bundle of 100 cigars, typically bound by a ribbon.
Factory processes for making cigars: rolling methods, bunching, blending, sorting, and quality control.
A rolling method in which the leaves are folded in a zig-zag shape like an accordion's bellows; faster than entubado, slower than booking.
The complete recipe of tobaccos in a premium cigar: up to five filler leaves, one or two binder leaves, and the exterior wrapper; precise ingredients are rarely revealed.
The process of smoking a cigar after its band has been removed, with no knowledge of the brand or blend.
A rolling method in which filler leaves are layered on top of one another like pages of a book and rolled up in a scroll; quick, but can create draw issues.
The combination of binder and filler leaves, placed in a mold and then finished with a wrapper leaf.
The factory worker who specializes in assembling the binder and filler leaves; distinct from the roller in many factories.
The process of grouping and rolling the filler leaves into a bunch before it is wrapped with the binder and wrapper.
related: cigars.Storage and Smoking.Draw; cigars.Storage and Smoking.Plugged

definition: A hand-powered machine with a leather pad, guides, and a metal lever that aids assembly of the bunch; common in the Dominican Republic, rare elsewhere, unknown in Cuba.
The flat piece of steel with a curved end that a cigar roller uses to trim a wrapper leaf to the correct size.
The owner of a cigar factory or brand; can also refer to a cigar roller.
The artisanal process of handcrafting a cigar: carefully arranging filler, binder, and wrapper leaves to ensure optimal construction and draw.
Among the last steps of production: trained workers examine each cigar against a stark black or white surface so every box exhibits a uniform color.
Removing the thick stems from tobacco leaves so they can be rolled: the entire stem for binder and wrapper leaves, the bottom two-thirds for filler.
A quality-control device that pulls air through a cigar to ensure it is rolled neither too tight nor too loose; widely relied upon since the 1990s.
A rolling method in which each filler leaf is rolled into a tube shape to ensure a perfect draw.
The cabinets at a cigar factory where freshly rolled cigars are cooled.
A head finish in which the roller extends and twists off the wrapper leaf instead of applying a traditional cap.
A tasteless, odorless substance used to apply the head of the wrapper leaf around the bunch in a handmade cigar.
A cigar made entirely by hand from premium long-filler tobaccos finished with a wrapper leaf.
A sheet of chopped tobacco scraps and cellulose adhesive, cut up for use in cheap machine-made cigars; never used in premium handmade cigars.
A person who reads to the cigar rollers while they make cigars; an uncommon practice today that survives in Cuba; the Montecristo brand traces its name to a lector's reading.
Whole-leaf tobacco used in premium handmade cigars, as opposed to chopped short-filler; called tripa in Spanish.
Cigars made by machine rather than by hand, using short-filler and homogenized tobacco; manufactured in far greater quantities than premium cigars.
A handmade cigar using a combination of long-filler and short-filler tobaccos.

The two-part wood or plastic form, joined under pressure, that conforms the bunch to the cigar shape being made; the word also names the harmful blue or green fungus that develops on cigars stored too warm — such cigars must be discarded.
A cigar blend that incorporates tobaccos from different countries, offering a diverse and layered smoking experience; the counterpart of a Puro.
A device used to compress cigar molds after bunching (hand-powered or pneumatic) or to compress tobacco bales after fermentation (hydraulic).
The factory worker who makes the cigar, applying the wrapper leaf to the bunch; in some factories one worker both bunches and rolls.
The area or floor of a cigar factory where rollers craft cigars by hand.
How a cigar is made: booking, the accordion method, or entubado.
The often wooden table where a cigar roller sits to make cigars.
Chopped-up tobacco scraps used predominantly in cheap machine-made cigars; burns hotter and faster than long filler.
The meticulous process of classifying cured tobacco leaves by size, texture, color, and quality before blending and rolling; broader than color sorting (escogida).
A cap with three seams; a Cuban style of finishing the head, now also used in Nicaragua, Honduras, and sometimes the Dominican Republic.
Post-harvest processing of tobacco leaves: curing, fermentation, and ageing.

The process of allowing tobacco to rest under precisely monitored conditions whereby unwanted impurities dissipate; applied to whole leaves in bales and to finished cigars, for months or several years.
The room in a cigar factory where rolled cigars are stored and allowed to rest so the tobaccos merge flavors; often made of Spanish cedar.
Present in freshly harvested tobacco leaves; proper curing and fermentation rid the leaves of it, and improperly aged cigars deliver a harsh, bitter taste from it.
A compressed, wrapped unit of storage for cured and fermented tobacco — often 100 pounds or more, aged for years or even decades.
Aging cigars in the original box in which they are packaged, which can exhibit distinctively uniform qualities of taste and aroma.
A climate-controlled curing barn delivering precise humidity and temperature through interior ductwork; uncommon due to expense and construction.
Charcoal (Spanish) used to raise the temperature in tobacco-curing barns; many operations now use propane heaters.
A plant pigment that replaces chlorophyll in tobacco as the chlorophyll naturally breaks down.
Re-moisturizing aged tobacco so it can be worked with, by dipping in water, misting, or high-humidity storage; also a term for flavoring pipe tobacco.
The wooden pole in a curing barn from which freshly harvested tobacco leaves hang; cuje cortos run about six feet, cuje largos twelve.
The process of gradually removing moisture from tobacco leaves after harvest, taking place in curing barns over roughly 45 days.
The structure where harvested tobacco is stored and dried gradually for roughly 45 days; temperature and humidity determine the curing time.
The top vent or opening of a tobacco curing barn where heat escapes and air flows.
The process of assembling a pilon or bulk of tobacco for fermentation.
The process of transferring harvested tobacco leaves from the fields to the curing barn.

The process after curing and before aging in which bulks of leaves release ammonia and other impurities under natural heat (up to 140 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure; can take several months or longer.
Workers in curing barns who continually monitor conditions as heat is introduced, to insure no fire starts; temperatures can exceed 150 degrees Fahrenheit.
Roughly 30 to 40 tobacco leaves tied together during the curing process; several hands are assembled into a bulk for fermentation.
A specialized ageing process applied to small batches of tobacco to enhance complexity and smoothness.
An additional fermentation step for tobacco from the periphery of a pilon, exposed to about 100 degrees Fahrenheit and 90% RH in a mulling room for a more complete fermentation.
A large pile (up to 4,000 pounds or more) of cured tobacco leaves assembled for fermentation; dismantled and reassembled several times over months.
A rudimentary structure used to cure tobacco in parts of the Dominican Republic; less protective than a traditional curing barn.
A string used to bind tobacco leaves together during the curing process.
Tobacco bales wrapped in palm bark, used to age fermented tobacco.
The long boards on Connecticut River Valley tobacco barns, designed to swing open to increase airflow.
Keeping and enjoying cigars: humidors, cutters, lighters, lighting technique, draw, burn behavior, and the smoking experience.
An electric or battery-powered device that expels and circulates humidity; typically used in larger humidors or cabinets.
The scent of a cigar, lit or unlit, as perceived by the olfactory senses.
A categorization tool used to describe and identify the different scents and flavor nuances in cigars, ranging from woody and spicy to floral and sweet.
Releasing an unwanted pocket of air from a butane lighter's fuel tank so a full injection of fresh fuel can occupy it; also called purging a lighter.
The practice of releasing trapped air and old butane from a jet-flame lighter before refilling, to ensure a cleaner, more efficient flame.
Harmless small white powdery dots, from crystallized natural oils, that appear on an aging cigar's wrapper — a sign of proper aging; not to be confused with harmful blue/green mold.
A clean-burning, odorless fuel preferred for cigar lighters; fuel refined at least five times is strongly recommended.
A burn defect where one portion of the cigar burns hotter and faster than the other; sometimes remedied by touching up the burn with a lighter.
Taking a draw on a cut but unlit cigar to preview its flavors before lighting.
The rate and efficiency at which a cigar burns, influenced by humidity, the tobacco blend, and construction.
The condition of taste when a cigar produces multiple transitions of flavor.
A tool used to clip or open the cap of a cigar so air can pass; the three most common are the straight (guillotine), punch (bullet), and V (cat's eye) cutters.
Dipping the head of a cigar into a drink, typically a darker spirit; often disapproved of by purists.
The process of pulling air through a cigar, or the pull itself; a measure of the cigar's construction, affected by the style of cut.
The final tasting notes of a cigar, or its residual taste on the palate; lingers longer in stronger cigars.
A cigar whose draw is too tight or that is rolled too densely.
A straight cutter that clips the cap off the head of a cigar.
Burning too fast or hot, typically of cigars rolled too loosely or under-filled.
The humidity source inside a humidor — traditionally floral foam in a vented plastic or metal case — replenished with distilled water or propylene glycol.
A box for storing cigars, often of Spanish cedar with a tight seal maintaining 65-70% relative humidity; also the room in a cigar shop where cigars are stored and displayed.
The device in a humidor that measures the humidity level; analog dial models persist alongside digital ones that also read temperature.
Drawing smoke into the lungs or diaphragm; common among cigarette smokers but never attempted with cigars.
A device for lighting cigars; butane models are preferred because refined butane exhibits fewer impurities and will not taint flavor.
Liquid fuel used in wick lighters; not recommended for cigars because it is unrefined and can taint the flavor.
A cigar that is under-filled, so too much air passes on the draw; burns hot and fast.
The amount of nicotine present in a cigar, influenced by the type and priming of the tobacco leaves used.
Pushing cigar smoke out through the nose, producing added layers of perceived flavor and aroma.
A humidification system that needs no batteries or electricity, such as traditional floral-foam units or Boveda packs.
A cutter with a sharp needle-like point that penetrates the cap to create airflow; can sometimes remedy a plugged cigar.
Having an obstructed draw; a piercer can sometimes loosen the tobacco, otherwise the cigar is unsmokable.
A 50/50 solution used to soak humidification units; designed to stop releasing humidity when the humidor reaches 70% RH, so cigars are not oversaturated.
A cutter with a circular blade that removes a precise section of the cap, keeping it intact; available in various ring gauges; use with careful, twisting pressure.
synonyms: Punch; bull's eye piercer; bullet cutter

definition: Blowing smoke from the head of a cigar out through the foot to eliminate the buildup of unwanted flavors.
Cigar-cutting scissors with sloping blades designed to embrace the cap of a Parejo without cracking the wrapper; folding models are pocket friendly.
The volume of smoke a cigar produces, which can indicate its construction quality and tobacco blend.
The ideal temperature at which a cigar should be enjoyed; overheating produces bitterness and harshness and can lead to tunnelling.
The duration a cigar burns: roughly 30 minutes for a 5x50 Robusto, over an hour for a 7.5x52 Double Corona; thinner cigars burn hotter and faster.
The portion of a cigar that tastes best — where flavor and strength harmonize perfectly on the palate; different for every cigar and smoker.
The process of slowly warming the foot of a cigar with a flame before lighting it, to ensure an even burn.
Lasioderma serricorne: a 2-3 millimeter beetle that hatches when the humidor temperature exceeds 72 degrees and ruins cigars with tiny pin-sized holes.
A butane lighter producing a concentrated single- or multiple-jet flame; convenient for toasting the foot quickly and performing touch-ups.
A burn defect where the inner filler leaves burn faster than the wrapper, often when too much time passes between draws; rotate the cigar to avoid it.
A cutter that carves a V-shape into the head, drawing smoke from the top and bottom of the cigar and concentrating it on the palate.
synonyms: V-cut; V-cutter; cat's eye; wedge cutter

definition: The best match for lighting a cigar: a long cedar match.
Growing tobacco: seeds, seedlings, primings, shade versus sun growing, and harvesting.
An airborne fungus (peronospora tabacina) that can infect and ruin an entire tobacco field in days; it has impacted every major growing region.
The material once used to cover shade-grown tobacco fields; today replaced by nylon.
A limited form of shading where barriers are erected only on the sides of the crop, protecting from wind and low-angle sun.
A tobacco varietal developed by crossing two or more plant types, engineered for disease resistance, greater yields, or specific flavor profiles.
The small leaves at the base of the tobacco plant; typically discarded.
The topmost filler priming; the thickest, heartiest, and strongest leaves because they receive the most sunlight.
related: cigars.Cigar Production.Blend; cigars.Storage and Smoking.Nicotine Strength

definition: The small leaves that grow at the very top of the plant; prized by cigar-makers for complex, intense flavor from maximum direct sunlight.
The most common plant of the genus Nicotiana, from which contemporary commercially grown tobacco derives; found only in cultivation.
history_note: 2026-11-20: the exactMatch mapping to Wikidata Q181095 (Nicotiana tabacum, species of plant), applied with ontology wave 2, was accidentally dropped from the term by a synonym update (an UPDATE_TERM that did not carry the term's conceptMappings — fixed in lakeloom the same day). This proposal restores it.

definition: Coated in a neutral material such as clay to make tiny tobacco seeds easier to handle.
The vertical stations of a tobacco plant, harvested bottom-up a few leaves at a time; from bottom: Volado, Seco, Viso, Ligero; leaves strengthen with height and sunlight.
The filler priming from the mid-section of the plant; the thinnest and mildest leaf used in the filler.
The bed where tobacco seedlings sprout; today often trays inside greenhouses, planted in excess as insurance against weather.
A young tobacco plant a few inches high, reached roughly 60 days after planting; transferred from tray or seedbed to the field.
Wrapper leaf grown under a tent (historically cheesecloth, now nylon) that filters sunlight, producing thinner, more elastic leaves; most associated with Connecticut.
A harvest method where the whole plant is cut at once rather than priming leaves in succession; associated with Connecticut Broadleaf and San Andrés.
An unwanted shoot removed from tobacco plants by workers so nutrients reach the leaves.
Tobacco grown in direct sunlight, yielding thicker leaves with stronger veins; fuller and stronger than shade grown; all filler tobacco is sun grown.
The tiny origin of the tobacco plant; often pelletized in clay for handling, with farmers collecting seeds from prized plants for future crops.
Removing the flowers, seeds, or upper portion of the plant so nutrients are redirected to the leaves, making them stronger and sweeter.
A tractor-towed implement that digs a channel and drops seedlings into the ground at worker stations; uncommon outside the Connecticut River Valley.
The filler priming below Ligero and above Seco; less intense than Ligero, stronger than Seco.
The filler priming near the bottom of the plant, under Seco; milder than Ligero and valued for its burning properties.
Laying stalk-cut tobacco on the ground to wilt in the sun after harvest.
Tobacco varieties, seed strains, and the regions and countries where cigar tobacco is grown.
A tobacco with dark, oily leaves grown in the northeastern coastal region of Brazil; its seeds are also grown in Ecuador.
An agricultural region of the Dominican Republic, roughly an hour from Santiago, where Fuente Fuente Opus X's Cuban-seed shade tobaccos were first harvested.
A West African nation well-known for producing a sought-after wrapper varietal; the term also classifies tobacco grown in the neighboring Central African Republic.
The Dominican valley in which much of the country's premium tobacco is planted.
One of Nicaragua's three key tobacco-growing regions, just north of Esteli, known for medium-bodied, rich tobacco.
A primary wrapper leaf grown in the Connecticut River Valley under direct sunlight, almost always processed as Maduro and harvested by stalk cutting.
A rare Cuban-seed wrapper grown in the Connecticut River Valley, known for its rich, leathery taste.
The primary tobacco-growing region of the US, from Hartford through Massachusetts; its fertile soils and growing techniques produce prized wrapper tobacco.
A silky, golden-blond wrapper grown under shade in the Connecticut River Valley, prized for its creamy, rich flavor.
The most prominent variety of Cuban-seed tobacco today, first introduced in the 1930s and now grown throughout Central America; no longer grown in Cuba due to disease susceptibility.
Tobaccos grown outside Cuba from seed varietals that originated there; Ecuador is a prominent region for Cuban-seed wrappers.
A nation regarded as one of the primary producers of premium cigars in the world; Santiago and La Romana account for much of its production.
A South American nation whose natural cloud cover and nutrient-rich volcanic soils produce prized wrapper leaves, chiefly outside Guayaquil in the Andes foothills.
The Nicaraguan town around which much of the country's cigar production is situated; its tobacco is the strongest of the three key regions.
Another term for a Cuban cigar.
The capital of Cuba; also a term often used to refer to Cuban cigars.
The fourth largest cigar-producing nation, behind Nicaragua, the Dominican Republic, and Cuba.
Slang for Cuba: the Island South of Miami.
One of Nicaragua's three key tobacco-growing regions; its refined tobacco is often used as wrapper and is the least intense of the three.
A key tobacco-growing valley in Honduras, near Danli.
A prized Brazilian wrapper leaf harvested near the Recôncavo region of the northeastern coast.
One of the world's most prominent cigar-producing and tobacco-growing nations; its three key regions are Esteli, Jalapa, and Condega, with production centered around Esteli.
A tobacco varietal grown in the Dominican Republic, used predominantly as binder and filler and known for its large leaves.
A volcanic island near Lake Nicaragua whose fertile volcanic soils yield tobacco with a distinctive sweet, earthy taste.
A region in Cuba where premium tobacco is grown.
Spanish for 'hair of gold': a tobacco prized for its rich, distinctive flavor; grown in Nicaragua and other regions but uncommon due to disease susceptibility.
A famous varietal of Cuban-seed tobacco grown in the Dominican Republic.
A world-famous tobacco-growing region in western Cuba where the country's most legendary and prized tobacco is grown.
Spanish for 'cigar'; specifically a cigar whose binder, filler, and wrapper tobaccos are all grown in one nation.
A Mexican wrapper leaf named for its growing region, stalk cut and typically dark brown, either oily or dry in texture; prized for rich, spicy, sweet taste.
A tobacco hybrid grown in the Dominican Republic.
The second largest city of the Dominican Republic and the area where most Dominican cigar production takes place.
A valley in western Cuba prized for the quality of tobacco grown there.
Cigar shapes and sizes: the named formats, from parejos such as Corona and Robusto to figurados such as Torpedo and Perfecto.
Among the largest standard cigar sizes, traditionally 9.25 inches by a 47 ring gauge; 'A' cigars can burn for as much as two hours.
A cigar shape similar to a Torpedo but shorter, with a more abrupt taper at the head.
A cigar with a flat, somewhat squared shape resulting from tight packing in a box with a flat top; degrees vary.
A rustic, often inexpensive cigar with an open foot and an open head; associated with Spaghetti Westerns.
A classic cigar shape measuring 7 inches by a 47 ring gauge, named for Sir Winston Churchill, history's most famous cigar smoker.
A small, thin, quick-burning machine-made cigar, usually of dry-cured short-filler tobacco, packaged in counts of ten or twenty.
A classic cigar size, typically 5 5/8 inches by a 42 ring gauge.
A 'fat' Corona, typically with a ring gauge over 50, approximating a traditional Toro in size.
Spanish for 'snake': three Panetelas (often 6 x 38) braided together and meant to be smoked individually; one origin theory is factory inventory control for rollers.
A large Figurado, usually at least 8 inches long, with a tapered head and closed foot; a common Diadema is the Salomon.
A long cigar size, typically 7.5 inches by a 49 to 52 ring gauge, providing an extended, cooler burn.
Any non-Parejo cigar shape, such as Torpedos, Belicosos, Pyramids, and Perfectos.
Spanish for 'fat'; a reference to thicker cigar shapes.
A Cuban cigar size measuring 5.5 inches by a 50 ring gauge.
A very long cigar size, typically 9.25 inches by a 47 ring gauge.
A long, narrow cigar size, traditionally 7 to 7.5 inches by a 38 ring gauge, noted for concentrated flavor.
A cigar shape measuring 6 to 7 inches by a 42 to 44 ring gauge; longer than a Corona, not as thin as a Panetela.
A long, slender cigar shape, typically 5 to 7 inches by a 34 to 38 ring gauge.
A cigar with straight, parallel sides, such as a traditional Robusto, Churchill, Toro, or Corona.
scope_note: Parejo is disjoint with Figurado (owl:disjointWith, axiom parejoDisjointWithFigurado): a cigar's shape class is either a Parejo — a cylindrical body with a straight, open foot — or a Figurado with some non-cylindrical element such as a tapered or pointed head. No shape is both, so classifying a cigar as one excludes the other.
history_note: 2026-11-20: the long-standing informal distinction from Figurado was formalised as the axiom parejoDisjointWithFigurado (owl:disjointWith), applied with the first ontology wave and first published in release v1.2.0.

definition: A cigar shape that tapers at both ends; all Perfectos are Figurados, but not all Figurados are Perfectos.
A smaller version of the Corona, approximately 4.5 to 5 inches by a 38 to 42 ring gauge.
A cigar shape that tapers sharply at the head with an open foot; often called a Torpedo.
The diameter of a cigar, measured in 64ths of an inch: a 50 ring gauge is 50/64 of an inch thick. Larger ring gauges generally burn cooler and can carry more complex blends.
related: cigars.Storage and Smoking.Draw; cigars.Storage and Smoking.Smoking Time

definition: The most popular cigar shape in the world, measuring 4.75 to 5.75 inches by a 48 to 52 ring gauge.
A large, curvaceous Figurado, typically 7.25 inches by a 57 ring gauge at its thickest point, tapered at the head and finished with a nipple at the foot; requires great skill to roll.
An extremely popular cigar size measuring 6 to 6.5 inches by a 50 to 54 ring gauge.
A cigar shape with a sharply tapering closed head; frequently interchanged with Pyramid.
A cigar shape whose fattest point is the foot, narrowing continually toward the head.
The most extreme method of pressing cigars into square shapes, using wooden slats between cigars for very sharp, squared-off edges; associated with the Padron Anniversary line.
A cigar's shape or size; Robusto, Churchill, Toro, and Corona are all vitolas.
scope_note: Dimensions of a vitola are expressed in inches (length) and 64ths of an inch (ring gauge); see the lengthInches and ringGauge attributes.

definition: The color spectrum of wrapper leaves, from Candela through Claro, Colorado, and Maduro to Oscuro.
A yellow cigar wrapper.
A green wrapper leaf produced by harvesting before full maturity and fire-curing quickly to lock in chlorophyll; known for mild, grassy, and sweet flavors.
synonyms: AMS; American Market Selection; Double Claro

definition: A pale wrapper leaf, from a light, faded green hue to a light tan.
A brown or reddish-brown color classification of wrapper leaves.
A wrapper shade darker than Colorado and lighter than Maduro, combining strength and sweetness with a typically richer taste.
Spanish for 'ripe': a very dark brown or nearly black wrapper, achieved through sun exposure or extended fermentation that brings sugars to the leaf surface.
A light-brown or golden-blond to medium-brown wrapper color; the modern term for what was once called English Market Selection or Colorado Claro; classic on Connecticut Shade.
synonyms: Colorado Claro; EMS; English Market Selection

definition: The darkest color of wrapper leaf, darker than Maduro, associated with pronounced intensity.
Spanish for 'rose-colored': Cuban-seed tobaccos exhibiting a reddish-brown color.
